PullRequest.Body:

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The changed duplicate parse, synchronous rendering call path, and per-update identity change are explicit in repository code. Exact milliseconds vary with response length and provider chunk frequency, but the extra full-input parse and allocation on each reached update are certain.
Findings.PerformanceResource: synchronous Markdown lexing CPU work and token-array allocations
Findings.PerformanceScaling: For a streamed response of final length N delivered across U updates, this adds one parse of the entire accumulated response on every visible-row rerender, adding O(U*N) aggregate work (quadratic when similarly sized chunks grow the response). The effective cardinality is one added lexer call per changed visible response row per update, not per conversation item.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: increased synchronous UI-thread CPU and allocation/GC pressure during streamed chat rendering, which can increase update latency and contribute to jank for long responses
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Each ARIA-label computation converted the response and lexed it once to count code blocks.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The added table count converts and lexes the same full response before the existing code-block lexer, so every ARIA-label computation now performs two complete Markdown tokenizations.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: RIGHT line 57 adds `marked.lexer(element.response.toString())` while the same method still executes the pre-existing full-response `marked.lexer(...)` at line 82, changing one tokenization per label computation into two.
Findings.Title: Reuse the Markdown tokenization for both counts
Findings.Impact: While a response streams, `ChatResponseViewModel` increments its model-change identity on every model update; `ChatWidget.onDidChangeItems` then replaces/renders that visible row, and `AccessibiltyRenderer.renderElement` synchronously calls this provider. Long, frequently updated responses therefore pay an extra full Markdown parse on the UI thread for every update, even when they contain no tables.
Findings.Evidence: `ChatResponseViewModel` increments `_modelChangeCount` in its model `onDidChange` listener and includes it in `dataId` (`chatViewModel.ts:426-429, 614`); `ChatWidget` handles each accumulated view-model change with `onDidChangeItems`, whose diff identity is `element.dataId` (`chatWidget.ts:961-970, 588-607`); replacement renders invoke `AccessibiltyRenderer.renderElement`, which calls `getAriaLabel` synchronously (`listWidget.ts:1281-1283`). In this method, added line 57 calls `marked.lexer(element.response.toString())`, and unchanged line 82 immediately repeats the same lexer call for code blocks.
Findings.Recommendation: Call `element.response.toString()` and `marked.lexer(...)` once, retain the token array, and derive both table and code-block counts from that shared result so ordering and label behavior remain unchanged.

Scenarios.CriticalPath: Each response-model update reaches the view-model change listener, `ChatWidget.onDidChangeItems`, tree row replacement/rendering, and synchronous ARIA-label computation before that render completes.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: One changed visible response row per streamed update; the parsed input is the full accumulated response, so cost grows with both update count and response length.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Updates are accumulated within a zero-delay event turn, then processed serially on the UI thread; there is no worker or limiter for label tokenization.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: There is no token cache or coalescing across updates. Each rendered identity performs two fresh `response.toString()`/Markdown lexer passes after the diff, versus one lexer pass before it.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: model updates increment the response identity, the widget renders the changed row, the accessibility renderer calls the provider synchronously, and the diff visibly duplicates the full lexer call.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Provider chunk rate and response lengths vary, so exact latency is workload-dependent; long generated answers and frequent chunks are realistic and magnify the cost.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable material amplification: the diff adds a second complete Markdown tokenization and token-array allocation per visible streamed update, increasing UI-thread CPU/GC pressure.

Scenarios.Scenario: Opening or restoring a chat with completed responses
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Visible rows receive ARIA labels synchronously as the object tree renders them; offscreen virtualized rows are outside the immediate critical path until scrolled into view.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number and Markdown length of visible/restored response rows; virtualization limits immediate cardinality to rendered rows.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Visible-row label computations are serial UI-thread work during tree rendering.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Cold and subsequent rerenders both tokenize each rendered response afresh; no shared tokenization exists between table and code-block counting.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for the duplicate synchronous parsing; moderate impact because virtualization bounds row cardinality.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The number of simultaneously rendered rows is bounded by the viewport, making this less severe than streaming despite potentially long historical responses.
Scenarios.Verdict: The same reported duplicate-parse mechanism applies, but viewport virtualization limits this scenario's fan-out.

Scenarios.Scenario: Focusing or navigating chat list responses
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Ordinary focus changes use existing row ARIA attributes; keyboard type navigation can call the provider for the focused element, but does not introduce subprocess, IPC, filesystem, database, or network work.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: At most the focused response per navigation event, with cost proportional to that response's Markdown length.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Synchronous and serial on the UI thread.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache; any direct provider call repeats both lexer passes. Existing rendered labels otherwise avoid recomputation on focus alone.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High that no external expensive boundary is reached and that any provider call duplicates tokenization.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Direct navigation-triggered provider calls are less frequent than streaming rerenders, so this is a secondary trigger.
Scenarios.Verdict: No separate finding beyond the shared-tokenization issue; event cardinality is low.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over the sole changed file and all diff pages. Traced list rendering, tree identity replacement, response-model updates, virtualization, cache behavior, concurrency, and transitive expensive boundaries. Submitted one medium-confidence-high finding for the added duplicate full Markdown parse on the streamed-render critical path; found no boundary fan-out, retention, cleanup, cache-lifecycle, or regression-fix signal.
